title: Maximilian Kolbe
hookLine: in Auschwitz a Polish priest offers his life in place of a father of a family

lines: A PRISONER STEPS OUT OF LINE.
cards: Roll call in Auschwitz, in summer heat. A prisoner from the block has escaped, and the rule is brutal: men from his block will be chosen to die by starvation in an underground cell.
The SS officer in charge walks the rows and points. One of the men picked, a Polish soldier named Franciszek Gajowniczek, cries out for his wife and his children.
Then a thin prisoner in glasses steps out of line and walks toward the officer.

teach.h: A FRIAR, A PRINTER, A PRISONER.
teach.b: The man was Maximilian Kolbe, a Polish Catholic priest and a Franciscan friar. Before the war he ran a large friary near Warsaw and printed magazines and newspapers, a busy, inventive man devoted to Mary.
The Nazis arrested him, and he ended up in Auschwitz, a prisoner with a number instead of a name.

teach.h: HE ASKS TO TAKE THE FATHER'S PLACE.
teach.b: At the roll call, by the accounts of survivors, he asked to take the place of the man with a family. Asked who he was, he said simply that he was a Catholic priest. The officer agreed.

Gajowniczek went back into the line, and Kolbe went down into the starvation cell with the others. Witnesses later said the cell, instead of screaming, was full of prayers and hymns, and that Kolbe led them.
He was among the last still alive, and the guards killed him by lethal injection. Gajowniczek survived the camp and spent the rest of his life telling people what had been done for him.

The Catholic Church has named Kolbe a saint, and the Gospel line people often connect with him is from John. In the King James Bible: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."
Kolbe hadn't been the man's friend. By the accounts, they were strangers. This week: remember them, for the Armenians.
The works of mercy. One Word, not a leader. Not cheap grace.
The beginning of life. The few who hid them. And now, let me go instead.

teach.h: A WEEK OF PEOPLE WHO PAID A COST.
teach.b: A week of people who paid a cost.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Maximilian Kolbe each August, and he is honored as a patron of prisoners and families; his story is often told at Masses and in schools that bear his name.

games.q: you're standing in the rows. a stranger next to you has just been chosen to die, and he's crying for his children. what do you do?
o: keep your eyes down and stay in line.
step out and ask to take his place.
whisper a prayer for him and stay still.
games.why: Kolbe stepped out, said he was a Catholic priest, and asked to take the father's place. the officer agreed.

practice: Nobody is asking for Kolbe's sacrifice; start much smaller. Who near you is carrying something you could carry instead: the colleague with the dull task, the parent who always does bedtime, the friend who always drives?
Picture stepping out of line and saying quietly, let me do that one, and if you pray, ask a blessing on them.

wordCard.voice: Maximilian Kolbe. A Polish friar who, in Auschwitz, asked to die in place of a man with a family, and was allowed to.

orig.note: Greek: for, on behalf of, in place of. John 15:13, lay down his life for his friends.

carryVoice: Your line: let me go instead. Love that steps out of line, even for a stranger. A heavy week, and you stayed with it.
